sources.headline: Tech allies rally behind Jensen Huang, calling him vital in AI race
sources.text: SAN FRANCISCO – Within hours of Jensen Huang’s admission on Nov 8 that he had been unfaithful to his wife, some of Silicon Valley’s most influential investors closed ranks around him.Their messages, delivered mostly on social media, were consistent. Huang’s relationship with a woman identified by US officials as a Chinese spy was a personal failing. Losing the Nvidia chief executive, they argued, would be a far bigger blow to the country, and America could not win the artificial intelligence race without him.“Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in a post on the afternoon of Nov 8. He said that Huang “did something incredibly dumb” and that it was bad for America, “but my guess is there was no bad intention”.He concluded that Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership”.About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post and added: “I agree.”The show of loyalty reflects Huang’s rarefied standing in Silicon Valley. In the three decades since he co-founded Nvidia, he has gone from running a maker of video game graphics cards to presiding over the company at the centre of the AI boom, now one of the world’s most valuable companies.Nvidia’s chips are the scarce resource every AI company needs, a position that makes Huang something of a kingmaker. Decisions about who gets his products, and how many, can shape which start-ups and tech giants pull ahead. Nvidia’s finances are also deeply intertwined with other leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.(China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)Bill Ackman, a billionaire hedge fund manager, called Jensen Huang “an incredible human” who took “full responsibility as he should” and urged people to “support him and his family”. Later on Nov 8, Ackman added that he was “not suggesting he gets a free pass”.On Nov 9, investor Gavin Baker argued that many venture capitalists were “patriotic Americans” who believed Huang’s policy views served the country against China. He wrote that it would be “a disaster for America – and a gift to China – if Jensen goes down”.“100% in agreement,” replied Jason Calacanis, a host of the “All-In” podcast, which is a popular podcast hosted by a group of venture capitalists including David Sacks, President Donald Trump’s former AI and crypto czar.Antonio Gracias, founder of Valor Equity Partners and a long-time associate of Musk, agreed on Nov 10: “America would not be ahead in the AI race without Jensen. He clearly made a mistake. One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership.”The “All-In” hosts have been close to Huang. During an appearance onstage with the podcast’s hosts in September, Huang took a phone call from Trump.Trump, too, has stood by Huang.“I really believe him,” he said on Nov 9, recalling a conversation when Huang told him he did not know that Alice Huang was a spy. The New York Times has reported that Trump was briefed a year ago about intelligence showing that she was an operative for the Chinese government. Trump on Nov 10 demurred when asked whether he received the briefing in 2025.Huang has been among Washington’s most forceful voices against cutting China off from American chips, and has been an ally of Trump since his return to office. That, Calacanis acknowledged, makes him and his company “a critical target, and we need to protect them both”.In Congress, the Republican leaders of three influential House committees have asked Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang.The Times reported in October that US officials had concluded that Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips, had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation and said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Beijing dismissed the allegations as smears. NYTIMESThis article originally appeared in The New York Times.

sources.headline: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
sources.text: The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models."Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand. It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little. But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech."President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work. China denies that she was engaged in espionage.Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest. Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy. He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.But can he survive?At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out. Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy. He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings. And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

Issued on: 09/11/2026 - 21:09

Nvidia chief Jensen Huang sits at the center of the artificial intelligence boom, and the spy scandal that erupted over the weekend threatens to shake the company at a time when confidence in the AI investment frenzy is already fragile. Taiwan-born Huang is regarded as the godfather of the AI economy, the executive every player in the industry must turn to because the technology depends on the graphics processing units (GPUs) that his company designs. FRANCE 24's Wassim Cornet reports from Los Angeles.

sources.headline: How could the Jensen Huang 'spy' scandal affect Nvidia's future?
sources.text:
Updated: 9 November 2026 - 19:57 GMT+1
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing scrutiny over alleged links to Chinese intelligence involving a businesswoman with whom he had an intimate relationship.
The company's board has launched an independent investigation into the matter. Nvidia says it has no reason to believe its trade secrets or US national security have been compromised.
The controversy has raised questions about the potential impact on the company and its investors. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co, says Huang has been central to Nvidia's success, particularly its shift towards artificial intelligence.
"Jensen's almost been a superhero for Nvidia's shareholders," Ives says, adding that many investors have come to view him differently from other corporate leaders.
Nvidia shares fell around 5% in premarket trading on Monday following news of the investigation.

The fallout from the Nvidia scandal may test the fragile truce between the US and China, analysts say, as calls in Washington grow to tighten semiconductor export controls just days before US President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China.
“I think that [scandal] could have a bigger impact down the line during the meeting in Miami or even further down the line,” said Ilaria Mazzocco, a senior fellow at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. Mazzocco was referring to another Trump-Xi meeting expected in December on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami.

Mazzocco added that the bilateral arrangement was underpinned by the leverage each country held over the other, particularly China’s dominance in rare earths, which could limit Washington’s room to tighten restrictions.

“It has the potential to deepen mistrust between the US and China at a sensitive moment in bilateral relations,” wrote George Chen, a Partner and Chair of Digital Practice at The Asia Group, in a Substack post.

However, some experts argue that the controversy is unlikely to have an immediate impact on the coming meeting during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, given Trump’s public backing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his continued efforts to build a closer relationship with Xi.
00:55
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits to extramarital affair; board orders investigation

“I really don’t see this as having a huge impact on the summit,” said Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Centre for Security and Emerging Technology.

Nvidia’s board launched a probe on Sunday after a New York Times report linked Huang to a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US intelligence officials of passing information to Beijing.

In a statement, Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife and would fully cooperate with the inquiry.

Beijing calls allegations ‘nothing but smears against China’
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the allegations “unsubstantiated” and said they amounted to “nothing but smears against China”.

Huang became a regular presence in Washington as Nvidia sought to sell its advanced chips to China, forging a close working relationship with Trump.

Several lawmakers and defence analysts have spent months opposing the Trump administration’s decision last year to permit sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China, the company’s second-best AI chips, warning the move compromises the push to contain Beijing’s AI ambitions.

The White House largely resisted calls for tougher oversight, as the administration sought to shield frequent Xi-Trump engagements and sustain the fragile trade truce negotiated in Busan, South Korea.

But with Huang – who aggressively lobbied to loosen those restrictions – now embroiled in an alleged espionage scandal, the fallout has refocused Congressional pressure on the administration to reverse course and impose tighter controls.

Lawmakers on Monday demanded an investigation and summoned Huang for a closed-door briefing on November 18.

“I’m pushing to investigate Jensen Huang and Nvidia to determine whether our national security was compromised,” Democratic Senator Chris Coons, who is also part of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote on social media.

However, analysts say Trump could still ignore the pressure to preserve his personal ties with Xi.

“Congress can only do so much to force his hand,” said Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser at the International Crisis Group.

“Trump has largely ignored its counsel to date, and he has given every indication that he intends to continue focusing on burnishing his rapport with Xi,” Wyne said.

WATCH: US President Donald Trump hosts state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping

Bresnick believed the scandal would give Democrats further impetus to tighten export control restrictions again, with Trump’s response closely watched.

“It’ll be interesting to see how that works and if Trump is going to veto any sort of harsher export control measures and whether there will be enough bipartisan pushback to overwhelm that veto,” he added.

Hilton Root, a professor of public policy at George Mason University, argued that while Congress has “substantial power,” it operates through “investigation and legislation.”

“In the immediate term, Congress’s strongest leverage may be to establish a public record of failures that makes continued approvals politically difficult,” he added.

As pressure mounts, Trump has publicly defended Huang, calling him an “honourable guy” who has “done such an incredible job”.

Trump said: “I asked him that question: Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really believe him.”

Huang remains influential figure in US-China technology race
Huang has emerged as a key figure in the US-China technology engagement. In May, he was invited at the last minute to join Trump for his trip to Beijing to visit Xi.

He travelled with the president on Air Force One to China as part of the US’ high-profile tech delegation. The summit marked the first visit by a US president in nearly a decade.

Additionally, when Xi visited the US in September, Huang and his wife Lori were invited to the White House state dinner and given a prime seat at the table with both Xi and Trump.
From left, Huang, his wife Lori Huang and Tim Cook, chairman of the board of directors of Apple, attend a state dinner hosted by Trump for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in Washington on September 24. Photo: Reuters

Trump said on Sunday he would still invite the Nvidia CEO on his coming trip to Asia, adding: “I’d certainly take him.”

Trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines from November 16 to 18 to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

He will then visit Shenzhen for the Apec meetings, where he is due to hold his third bilateral meeting of the year with Xi.

“It doesn’t seem like this [scandal] is affecting president Trump’s confidence in Jensen Huang,” Mazzocco said.

Bresnick predicts that Trump’s view on Huang could change over time, depending on what comes next.

“I assume people on his staff will be trying to pry him away from Huang. The way that I see Trump making decisions is that when things get too toxic, he will finally distance himself,” said Bresnick.

“That could happen as we go forward here, and as investigations reveal other things, we could see Trump say, OK, maybe it’s politically too costly to align myself with this guy.”

Nayan Seth
